rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Metaphor has three pillars: the borrowed expression, the source meaning from which it is borrowed, and the shared meaning joining source and target.
rows.anchor: أركان الاستعارة ثلاثة مستعار وهو لفظ المشبه به ومستعار منه وهو معنى اللفظ المشبه ومستعار له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One class uses a perceptible image for another perceptible thing through a perceptible common feature: spreading fire for gray hair, waves for turbulent movement, and breath for dawn's gradual light.
rows.anchor: أحدها استعارة محسوس لمحسوس بوجه محسوس نحو

rows.speaker: ابن أبي الإصبع
rows.claim: Ibn Abi al-Isba calls metaphor from perceptible to perceptible through an intellectual feature subtler; here harvested vegetation evokes destruction, an intellectual common feature.
rows.anchor: قال ابن أبي الإصبع وهي ألطف من الأولى

rows.speaker: ابن أبي الإصبع
rows.claim: Ibn Abi al-Isba calls abstract-for-abstract metaphor through an intellectual feature the subtlest: sleep stands for death because neither displays activity, and anger is described as falling silent.
rows.anchor: قال ابن أبي الإصبع وهي ألطف الاستعارات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A perceptible term is borrowed for an abstract experience: touching, originally physical, describes undergoing hardship; the shared feature is reaching or affecting someone.
rows.anchor: استعير المس وهو حقيقة في الأجسام وهو محسوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition fī has ten listed senses: place or time, accompaniment, cause, superposition, bi, ilā, min, ʿan, comparison, and emphasis; here it emphasizes the command, meaning ride it.
rows.anchor: عاشرها التوكيد وهي الزائدة نحو

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Custom can establish an ellipsis when the literal wording is implausible: Mujahid supplies ‘a place for fighting,’ since the speakers knew warfare and had urged the Prophet not to leave Medina.
rows.anchor: والمراد مكانا صالحا للقتال وإنما كان كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the basmala, infer the act being begun—such as ‘I read’ or ‘I eat’; rhetoricians agree, against grammarians who estimate ‘I begin’ or ‘my beginning.’
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا أهل البيان قاطبة خلافا لقول النحاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatical form may require omitted wording: ‘I swear’ is supplied after lā uqsim, while lā is supplied in tالله تفتأ because an affirmative answer would take the oath lām and nūn.
rows.anchor: لأنه لو كان الجواب مثبتا دخلت اللام والنون كقوله

rows.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
rows.claim: Grammarians supply ‘existent’ as the predicate of lā ilāha illā Allāh; Fakhr al-Din al-Razi rejects the needed ellipsis and says their restricted negation is faulty.
rows.anchor: وقد أنكره الإمام فخر الدين وقال هذا الكلام لا يحتاج إلى تقدير وتقدير النحاة فاسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reply is that supplying ‘existent’ entails excluding every deity other than God; since nonexistence is not at issue, the construction in effect negates deity absolutely.
rows.anchor: فإن العدم لا كلام فيه فهو في الحقيقة نفي للحقيقة مطلقة لا مقيدة

words: وما نحن بتاركي آلهتنا عن قولك وما نحن لك بمؤمنين
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concision can arise from restriction, conjunction, passive voice, pronouns, a verb governing a complement clause, ellipsis in coordination or objects, interrogative and conditional particles, generic words, and dual or plural forms.
rows.anchor: أن من أنواع إيجاز القصر باب الحصر سواء كان بإلا أو بإنما

rows.speaker: ابن أبي الإصبع
rows.claim: Ibn Abi al-Isba also counts interpretive breadth as a form of concision: wording supports several possible meanings, as with the openings of sūras.
rows.anchor: مما يصلح أن يعد من أنواعه المسمى بالاتساع من أنواع البديع وهو أن يؤتى بكلام يتسع فيه التأويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment lists consonant assimilation examples: sīn into zāy, shīn into sīn, and ḍād into shīn, each in the cited phrase only.
rows.anchor: والسين في الزاي في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāf assimilates into kāf after a vowel and also in one word before mīm; kāf assimilates into qāf after a vowel, except when its preceding letter is still.
rows.anchor: والقاف في الكاف إذا ما تحرك ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lām assimilates into rā after a vowel or after a still letter when lām is u- or i-voweled; it does not after fatḥa, except lām in qāla, which assimilates wherever it occurs.
rows.anchor: واللام في الراء إذا تحرك ما قبلها

rows.speaker: ابن الجزري
rows.claim: Mīm before bā is hidden with nasalization after a vowel, but pronounced clearly after sukūn; Ibn al-Jazari says listing this as idghām, as earlier scholars did, is incorrect because it is ikhfāʾ.
rows.anchor: وهذا نوع من الإخفاء المذكور في الترجمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nūn assimilates into rā or lām after a vowel and is otherwise clear, except nūn in naḥnu, which assimilates because it recurs often, repeats nūn, stays vocalized, and is heavy.
rows.anchor: لكثرة دورها وتكرار النون فيها ولزوم حركتها وثقلها

words: أو أن نفعل في أموالنا ما نشاء
rows.speaker: ابن هشام
rows.claim: Ibn Hisham rejects coordinating أن نفعل with أن نترك: the speakers are not told to do as they wish; it coordinates with ما, so the sense is leaving both ancestral worship and their chosen financial conduct.
rows.anchor: قال ابن هشام وقد زلت أقدام كثير من المعربين راعوا في الإعراب ظاهر اللفظ ولم ينظروا في موجب المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parsing Thamūd as a fronted object before mā is impossible because a negative mā takes sentence-initial position; read it as coordinated with ʿĀd or supply ‘and He destroyed Thamūd.’
rows.anchor: إن ثمودا مفعول مقدم وهذا ممتنع لأن ل ما النافية الصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In lā ʿāṣim al-yawm and lā tathrīb ʿalaykum al-yawm, al-yawm cannot modify the noun of lā, which would then require accusative nunation; it modifies an omitted element.
rows.anchor: إن اسم لا حينئذ مطول فيجب نصبه وتنوينه وإنما هو متعلق بمحذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the queen’s question, the bāʾ is not attached to nāẓirah, as al-Ḥawfī says, because an interrogative has precedence; it attaches to the following verb.
rows.anchor: بل هو متعلق بما بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional أينما ثقفوا has precedence, so ملعونين is not a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of ثقفوا or أُخذوا; it is an accusative of censure.
rows.anchor: باطل لأن الشرط له الصدر بل هو منصوب على الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti rejects Abu ʿUbayda’s claim that kāf is an oath particle: Arabic supplies no such use, and attaching the relative ما to an overt subject is poetic; he prefers an omitted predicate comparing the two disliked situations.
rows.anchor: ويبطله أن الكاف لم تجئ بمعنى واو القسم

rows.speaker: ابن مهران
rows.claim: Ibn Mihrān wrongly explains the doubled tāʾ as an added prefix; the reading is feminine singular البقرة تشابهت, with the two tāʾs assimilated across the word boundary.
rows.anchor: ولا حقيقة لهذه القاعدة وإنما أصل القراءة

rows.speaker: نوف الشامي
rows.claim: Nawf al-Shāmī says Ṣāliḥ was an Arab; after ʿĀd’s destruction Thamūd settled after them, and God sent Ṣāliḥ as a youth, who preached until old age; only Hūd and Ṣāliḥ were prophets between Noah and Abraham.
rows.anchor: وقال نوف الشامي صالح من العرب لما أهلك الله عادا عمرت ثمود بعدها فبعث الله إليهم صالحا غلاما شابا

rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥajar and others say the Qur’an indicates that Thamūd followed ʿĀd just as ʿĀd followed Noah.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن حجر وغيره القرآن يدل على أن ثمودا كان بعد عاد كما كان عاد بعد قوم نوح

rows.speaker: الثعلبي عن النووي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī, quoting al-Nawawī’s Tahdhīb, gives Ṣāliḥ’s genealogy, says he was sent young to an Arab people between the Ḥijāz and Syria, stayed twenty years, and died in Mecca aged fifty-eight.
rows.anchor: وقال الثعلبي ونقله عن النووي في تهذيبه ومن خطه نقلت هو صالح بن عبيد بن أسيف بن ماشج

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq gives Shuʿayb’s father as Mīkāʾīl; another reported genealogy names Malkāyān.
rows.anchor: قال ابن إسحاق هو ابن ميكاييل كذا بخط الذهبي في اختصار المستدرك وقال غيره ابن ملكاين

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Al-Nawawī’s handwritten Tahdhīb gives Shuʿayb’s lineage through Mīkāʾīl, Yashjan, Midyan, and Abraham; he was called the orator of the prophets, sent to Madyan and the People of the Thicket, prayed much, and became blind late in life.
rows.anchor: ورأيت بخط النووي في تهذيبه ابن ميكيل بن يشجن بن مدين بن إبراهيم الخليل كان يقال له خطيب الأنبياء

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: A group, including Ibn Kathīr, holds that Madyan and the People of the Thicket were one people; Ibn Kathīr argues both were exhorted to give full measure and weight.
rows.anchor: قال ابن كثير ويدل لذلك أن كلا منهما وعظ بوفاء المكيال والميزان

rows.speaker: السدي وعكرمة
rows.claim: Al-Suddī and ʿIkrimah report Shuʿayb was sent twice, first to Madyan destroyed by the Cry and then to the People of the Thicket destroyed by the shade, supporting distinct communities.
rows.anchor: واحتج الأول بما أخرجه عن السدي وعكرمة قالا ما بعث الله نبيا مرتين إلا شعيبا مرة إلى مدين

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAsākir transmits a raised report from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr that Madyan and the People of the Thicket were two peoples sent Shuʿayb; Ibn Kathīr calls it unusual and questions its attribution to the Prophet. Others posit a third people, the People of al-Rass.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن عساكر في تاريخه من حديث عبد الله بن عمرو مرفوعا أن قوم مدين وأصحاب الأيكة أمتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mūsā is identified as son of ʿImrān through Yaʿqūb, with no disagreement reported about his lineage; his name is Syriac.
rows.anchor: موسى هو ابن عمران يصهر بن قاهث بن لاوي بن يعقوب عليه السلام لاخلاف في نسبه وهو اسم سرياني

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says Mūsā was named for being cast between water and a tree: in Coptic, water is mū and tree is sā.
rows.anchor: وأخرج أبو الشيخ من طريق عكرمة عن ابن عباس قال إنما سمى موسى لأنه ألقي بين شجر وماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording treats their desire for gods besides God as rejected without making that desire an exclusive claim.
rows.anchor: المنكر إرادتهم آلهة دون الله من غير حصر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says fronting ‘the Hereafter’ and placing ‘they’ before ‘are certain’ indirectly criticizes the People of the Book: their afterlife belief is not true certainty, unlike believers in both revelations.
rows.anchor: وقد قال الزمخشري في ﴿ وبالآخرة هم يوقنون ﴾

rows.speaker: المعترض
rows.claim: An objector says fronting الآخرة restricts their certainty to the Hereafter and fronting هم makes this restriction exclusive to them, implying Muslims believe only in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: وقد اعترض عليه بعضهم فقال تقديم ( الآخرة ) أفاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti calls the objection an odd inference from a supposed exclusivity of fronting, which he denies; even if accepted, fronting-induced restriction differs from explicit restriction.
rows.anchor: وهذا فهم عجيب ألجأه إليه فهمه الحصر وهو ممنوع وعلى تقدير تسليمه فالحصر على ثلاثة أقسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restriction by mā…illā explicitly excludes others; Al-Suyuti prefers analyzing affirmation for Zayd as implication, since excluding non-action is not identical to asserting action, though it entails it.
rows.anchor: صريح في نفي القيام عن غير زيد ويقتضي إثبات القيام لزيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restriction with innamā resembles mā…illā but makes the positive assertion more explicit: Zayd’s action is stated directly and exclusion of others is inferred.
rows.anchor: وهو قريب من الأول فيما نحن فيه وإن كان جانب الإثبات فيه أظهر

words: الزاني لا ينكح إلا زانية أو مشركة
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restriction inferred from fronting is weaker: it leaves implied meanings untouched. Thus the first marriage rule implies chaste men may marry others but is silent about an adulteress, clarified by the next rule.
rows.anchor: الثالث الحصر الذي قد يفيده التقديم وليس هو على تقدير تسليمه مثل الحصرين الأولين

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says two inheritance verses on kalālah came down, one in winter at the beginning of al-Nisāʾ and one in summer at its end.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي أنزل الله في الكلالة آيتين إحداهما في الشتاء وهي التي في أول النساء والأخرى في الصيف

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, ʿUmar says he repeatedly questioned the Prophet about kalālah, who responded sternly and pointed to the summer verse at the end of al-Nisāʾ as sufficient.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح مسلم عن عمر ما راجعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في شيء ما راجعته في الكلالة

words: يستفتونك قل الله يفتيكم في الكلالة
rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report in al-Mustadrak has the Prophet answer a question about kalālah by citing the summer verse; revelation during the Farewell Pilgrimage is classified as summer, including the start of al-Māʾidah, ‘Today I perfected,’ the debt verse, and al-Naṣr.
rows.anchor: وفي المستدرك عن أبي هريرة أن رجلا قال يا رسول الله ما الكلالة قال أما سمعت الآية التي نزلت في الصيف

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Tabūk revelation is classed as summer because the expedition occurred in extreme heat. A report says the Prophet announced Rome as the destination; Jad ibn Qays sought leave fearing temptation by Roman women, and a hypocrite objected to the heat, prompting two verses.
rows.anchor: ومنه الآيات النازلة في غزوة تبوك فقد كانت في شدة الحر

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report in Ṣaḥīḥ from ʿĀʾishah says the verses about the false accusation, through ‘and a generous provision,’ were revealed on a winter day.
rows.anchor: ففي الصحيح عن عائشة أنها نزلت في يوم شات

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: The al-Aḥzāb verses are classed as winter revelation. In Ḥudhayfah’s report, people left the Prophet during a cold night except twelve; he sent Ḥudhayfah to the enemy camp, and the account says the verses beginning ‘Remember God’s favor’ were revealed.
rows.anchor: والآيات التي في غزوة الخندق من سورة الأحزاب فقد كانت في البرد ففي حديث حذيفة تفرق الناس عن رسول الله

words: من ذا الذي يقرض الله قرضا حسنا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can entice, as in asking who will lend God a goodly loan or whether listeners should be shown a trade that saves them.
rows.anchor: السادس عشر الترغيب نحو ﴿ من ذا الذي يقرض الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can function as prohibition: ‘What deceived you by your generous Lord?’ means do not be deceived; other examples command fear of God rather than people.
rows.anchor: السابع عشر النهي نحو ﴿ أتخشونهم فالله أحق أن تخشوه ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A question from a subordinate to a superior can be supplication, functioning like a prohibition: ‘Do not destroy us for what the foolish did.’
rows.anchor: الثامن عشر الدعاء وهو كالنهي إلا أنه من الأدنى إلى الأعلى نحو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can seek guidance, as in the angels’ question about placing a corrupter on earth.
rows.anchor: التاسع عشر الاسترشاد نحو ﴿ أتجعل فيها من يفسد فيها ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can express a wish, as in asking whether there are any intercessors.
rows.anchor: العشرون التمني نحو ﴿ فهل لنا من شفعاء ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can express impatience or longing for an outcome, as in ‘When will God’s help come?’
rows.anchor: الحادي والعشرون الاستبطاء نحو ﴿ متى نصر الله ﴾

words: ألا تحبون أن يغفر الله لكم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can gently invite someone to act, as in asking whether they would not love God to forgive them.
rows.anchor: الثاني والعشرون العرض نحو ﴿ ألا تحبون أن يغفر الله لكم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can urge or incite action, as in asking why the believers do not fight oath-breakers.
rows.anchor: الثالث والعشرون التحضيض نحو ﴿ ألا تقاتلون قوما نكثوا أيمانهم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can feign ignorance or ask in a way that challenges an assertion, as in asking whether the Reminder was sent to him alone.
rows.anchor: الرابع والعشرون التجاهل نحو ﴿ أأنزل عليه الذكر من بيننا ﴾

words: من ذا الذي يشفع عنده إلا بإذنه
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can magnify or exalt the subject, as in asking who could intercede with God without His permission.
rows.anchor: الخامس والعشرون التعظيم نحو ﴿ من ذا الذي يشفع عنده إلا بإذنه ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can belittle or mock; the Quraysh’s ‘Is this the one God sent as messenger?’ is an example, as is ‘Is this the one who mentions your gods?’
rows.anchor: السادس والعشرون التحقير نحو ﴿ أهذا الذي يذكر آلهتكم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can imply that a point is sufficient or needs no further statement, as in the question about Hell as the arrogant’s dwelling.
rows.anchor: السابع والعشرون الاكتفاء نحو ﴿ أليس في جهنم مثوى للمتكبرين ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can present something as remote or implausible, as in asking how the reminder could benefit him then.
rows.anchor: الثامن والعشرون الاستبعاد نحو ﴿ وأنى له الذكرى ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can reassure or put the addressee at ease, as in Moses being asked what he holds in his right hand.
rows.anchor: التاسع والعشرون الإيناس نحو ﴿ وما تلك بيمينك يا موسى ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Interrogation can be sarcastic or mocking: the people of Shuʿayb deride his prayer, and Abraham asks why the idols neither eat nor speak.
rows.anchor: الثلاثون التهكم والاستهزاء نحو ﴿ أصلاتك تأمرك ﴾

rows.speaker: الموفق عبد اللطيف البغدادي
rows.claim: Al-Muwaffaq ʿAbd al-Laṭīf al-Baghdādī reads the repeated interrogative as emphasis after a long clause: the first question sets up a conditional, and its answer is that the condemned cannot be rescued.
rows.anchor: قال الموفق عبد اللطيف البغدادي أي من حق عليه كلمة العذاب فإنك لا تنقذه فمن للشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamkīn prepares a sentence ending so it fits securely and completes the meaning; removing it disrupts understanding. Here ‘forbearing’ suits worship and ‘right-minded’ suits financial conduct.
rows.anchor: فالتمكين ويسمى ائتلاف القافية أن يمهد الناثر للقرينة أو الشاعر للقافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending ‘do they not hear?’ fits reports about earlier peoples, which are heard; the companion passage about water is visual and ends ‘do they not see?’
rows.anchor: لأنه الموعظة فيها مسموعة وهي أخبار القرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘vision does not perceive Him, while He perceives vision,’ al-Laṭīf fits what sight cannot perceive and al-Khabīr fits what He perceives.
rows.anchor: فإن اللطف يناسب ما لا يدرك بالبصر والخبر يناسب ما يدركه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending ‘blessed is God, the best of creators’ is perfectly fitted to the preceding account of human creation.
rows.anchor: فإن في هذه الفاصلة التمكين التام المناسب لما قبلها

rows.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Thābit reports that Muʿādh ibn Jabal supplied the verse’s final phrase before hearing the revelation finished; the Prophet laughed and said, ‘With it I ended.’
rows.anchor: فأخرج ابن أبي حاتم من طريق الشعبي عن زيد بن ثابت قال أملى علي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An Arab heard an unlearned reader end the warning about slipping with ‘forgiving, merciful’ and objected that God would not say that; after correction to ‘mighty, wise,’ he said this ending fits because mercy there might encourage wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: قال إن كان هذا كلام الله فلا يقول كذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall’s leaning toward collapse is likened to a living being turning aside, so it is given will, a quality proper to rational beings.
rows.anchor: شبه ميلانه للسقوط بانحراف الحي فأثبت له الإرادة التي هي من خواص العقلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment also cites ‘touching hardship’ and ‘Who raised us from our resting place?’ as examples of explicit metaphor.
rows.anchor: ومن التصريحية آية ﴿ مستهم البأساء ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A concordant metaphor joins meanings that can coexist: making someone alive represents guiding the lost, and life and guidance could meet in one thing.
rows.anchor: أي ضالا فهديناه استعير الإحياء من جعل الشيء حيا للهداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An oppositional metaphor joins meanings that cannot coexist; its taunting subtypes use a word for its opposite, as in ‘glad tidings’ for warning, ironic praise of Shuʿayb’s opponents, and ‘the mighty, noble’ for humiliation.
rows.anchor: ومن العنادية التهكمية والتمليحية وهما ما استعمل في ضد أو نقيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A representational metaphor draws its likeness from several features: trusting God for protection and escape from harm resembles holding a strong rope suspended from above and safe from breaking.
rows.anchor: شبه استظهار العبد بالله ووثوقه بحمايته والنجاة من المكارة باستمساك

words: وما توفيقي إلا بالله عليه توكلت وإليه أنيب
rows.speaker: الزركشي
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashī’s inventory of Qur’anic sciences includes abrogation, ambiguous and decisive verses, divine attributes, inimitability, transmitted recitation, the Sunnah’s support, exegesis, forms of address, literal and figurative language, allusion, styles, and particles.
rows.anchor: الرابع والثلاثون معرفة ناسخه ومنسوخه الخامس والثلاثون معرفة موهم المختلف السادس والثلاثون معرفة المحكم من المتشابه

rows.speaker: الزركشي
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashī says exhaustive treatment of any field would consume a lifetime; his book therefore gives core principles and selected chapters because the discipline is long and life short.
rows.anchor: واعلم أنه ما من نوع من هذه الأنواع إلا ولو أراد الإنسان استقصاءه لاستفرغ عمره ثم لم يحكم أمره

words: وما توفيقي إلا بالله عليه توكلت وإليه أنيب
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti says reading al-Burhān inspired him to complete al-Itqān; he reordered and expanded its topics and made it an introduction to his planned major tafsir, Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn wa Maṭlaʿ al-Badrayn.
rows.anchor: ولما وقفت على هذا الكتاب ازددت به سرورا وحمدت الله كثيرا وقوي العزم على إبراز ما أضمرته
